opening.text: Picture a locked door. You have knocked on it. You have pushed on it. It will not open. Every person who has ever lived stands before that door. We call it death. No one has the key.
But one person does. Jesus Christ holds the keys of death. Because He holds them, the door is not a wall. It is a doorway.
Today I want to talk about the Resurrection of Jesus Christ. It is the best news the world has ever heard. And it is true.

mainMessage.text: Jesus Christ died. On the third day He rose from the grave with a perfect, living body. Because He did, every person who has ever lived will rise too. Death is not the end. That is why we can find peace when someone we love dies. It is why we can face our own death without terror. And it is why we can hope that whatever is broken in us now will one day be made whole.

blocks.text: The tomb was empty.

On the first day of the week, some women went to the tomb very early. They carried spices. They expected to care for a body. They did not expect what they found. The stone was rolled away, and the tomb was empty. Two angels asked them a question that still reaches us today.

Now upon the first day of the week, very early in the morning, they came unto the sepulchre, bringing the spices which they had prepared, and certain others with them. And they found the stone rolled away from the sepulchre. And they entered in, and found not the body of the Lord Jesus. And it came to pass, as they were much perplexed thereabout, behold, two men stood by them in shining garments: And as they were afraid, and bowed down their faces to the earth, they said unto them, Why seek ye the living among the dead? He is not here, but is risen: remember how he spake unto you when he was yet in Galilee,
Why could Jesus do what no one else could? Elder Russell M. Nelson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles explained it in his talk “Constancy amid Change” from the October 1993 general conference.

According to eternal law, that atonement required a personal sacrifice by an immortal being not subject to death. Yet He must die and take up His own body again. The Savior was the only one who could accomplish this. From His mother He inherited power to die. From His Father He obtained power over death.
He had power to die from His mother. He had power over death from His Father. No one else holds both. That is why the key belongs to Him alone.
He rose with a real body.

The Resurrection was not a ghost story. When Jesus stood among His disciples, they were terrified. They thought they were seeing a spirit. So He did something simple. He showed them His hands and His feet.

And as they thus spake, Jesus himself stood in the midst of them, and saith unto them, Peace be unto you. But they were terrified and affrighted, and supposed that they had seen a spirit. And he said unto them, Why are ye troubled? and why do thoughts arise in your hearts? Behold my hands and my feet, that it is I myself: handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have.
One of the Twelve, Thomas, was not there that night. He said he would not believe unless he could touch the wounds himself. A week later Jesus came again.

Then saith he to Thomas, Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing. And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God. Jesus saith unto him, Thomas, because thou hast seen me, thou hast believed: blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed.
Elder Joseph B. Wirthlin of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this in his talk “Christians in Belief and Action” from the October 1996 general conference.

The Atonement of Jesus Christ, an act of pure love, overcame the effects of the Fall and provided the way for all mankind to return to the presence of God. As part of the Atonement, the Savior overcame physical death and provided immortality for every one of God’s children through the Resurrection. He also overcame spiritual death and provided the possibility of eternal life, the life that God lives and the greatest of all the gifts of God.
Notice the words “every one of God’s children.” The gift is not small. It is not for a few. It is for all.
Everyone will rise.
The key Christ holds does not open one door. It opens every door. The Book of Mormon teaches this plainly. A day is coming when the spirit and the body will be joined again, for every person.

Now, there is a death which is called a temporal death; and the death of Christ shall loose the bands of this temporal death, that all shall be raised from this temporal death. The spirit and the body shall be reunited again in its perfect form; both limb and joint shall be restored to its proper frame, even as we now are at this time; and we shall be brought to stand before God, knowing even as we know now, and have a bright recollection of all our guilt. Now, this restoration shall come to all, both old and young, both bond and free, both male and female, both the wicked and the righteous; and even there shall not so much as a hair of their heads be lost; but every thing shall be restored to its perfect frame, as it is now, or in the body, and shall be brought and be arraigned before the bar of Christ the Son, and God the Father, and the Holy Spirit, which is one Eternal God, to be judged according to their works, whether they be good or whether they be evil.

The soul shall be restored to the body, and the body to the soul; yea, and every limb and joint shall be restored to its body; yea, even a hair of the head shall not be lost; but all things shall be restored to their proper and perfect frame.
Elder Dallin H. Oaks of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles spoke about this in his talk “All Men Everywhere” from the April 2006 general conference.

We . . . read that ‘his blood atoneth for the sins of those . . . who have died not knowing the will of God concerning them, or who have ignorantly sinned’ (Mosiah 3:11). Similarly, ‘the blood of Christ atoneth for \[little children\]’ (Mosiah 3:16). These teachings that the resurrecting and cleansing power of the Atonement is for all contradict the assertion that the grace of God saves only a chosen few. His grace is for all. These teachings of the Book of Mormon expand our vision and enlarge our understanding of the all-encompassing love of God and the universal effect of His Atonement for all men everywhere.
Not even a hair of the head will be lost. That is how complete this gift is.
Death lost its sting.
We grieve because death hurts. The scriptures do not hide that. But they also say that the hurt will not last. Abinadi and Paul both taught that the grave has no victory.

And if Christ had not risen from the dead, or have broken the bands of death that the grave should have no victory, and that death should have no sting, there could have been no resurrection. But there is a resurrection, therefore the grave hath no victory, and the sting of death is swallowed up in Christ.

So when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory. O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory? The sting of death is sin; and the strength of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.
Elder Russell M. Nelson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this in his talk “Now Is the Time to Prepare” from the April 2005 general conference.

Brothers and sisters, we live to die and we die to live—in another realm. If we are well prepared, death brings no terror. From an eternal perspective, death is premature only for those who are not prepared to meet God. Now is the time to prepare. Then, when death comes, we can move toward the celestial glory that Heavenly Father has prepared for His faithful children. Meanwhile, for sorrowing loved ones left behind . . . the sting of death is soothed by a steadfast faith in Christ, a perfect brightness of hope, a love of God and of all men, and a deep desire to serve them.
The sting is not gone because we do not feel loss. It is gone because loss is not the last word.
We will be whole again.

Many of us carry something broken. A body that hurts. A mind that is tired. A limb that does not work as it should. The Resurrection speaks to that. In the spirit world, the Savior’s work was already looking ahead to the day when the body would be restored.

Their sleeping dust was to be restored unto its perfect frame, bone to his bone, and the sinews and the flesh upon them, the spirit and the body to be united never again to be divided, that they might receive a fulness of joy.
Elder Russell M. Nelson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this in his talk “Perfection Pending” from the October 1995 general conference.

We need not be dismayed if our earnest efforts toward perfection now seem so arduous and endless. Perfection is pending. It can come in full only after the Resurrection and only through the Lord. It awaits all who love him and keep his commandments.
That should lift a weight. We are not asked to be finished today. Perfection is pending. It is coming.
He is the resurrection and the life.
Jesus did not only rise. He said that He is the resurrection. When Martha grieved for her brother, He gave her this promise.

Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live: And whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die. Believest thou this?
Paul wrote that Christ is the first of many.

But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept. For since by man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.
Elder D. Todd Christofferson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this in his talk “The Blessing of Scripture” from the April 2010 general conference.

The central purpose of all scripture is to fill our souls with faith in God the Father and in His Son, Jesus Christ—faith that They exist; faith in the Father’s plan for our immortality and eternal life; faith in the Atonement and Resurrection of Jesus Christ, which animates this plan of happiness; faith to make the gospel of Jesus Christ our way of life; and faith to come to know ‘the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom \[He has\] sent’ (John 17:3).
The Resurrection is what makes the plan work. Without it, the rest has no ending. With it, the plan has a glorious one.

story.title: The road to Emmaus

blocks.text: Two disciples walked home from Jerusalem three days after the Crucifixion. They were heartbroken. They had heard talk that the tomb was empty, but they could not yet believe it. A stranger joined them on the road, and they did not know Him.

And, behold, two of them went that same day to a village called Emmaus, which was from Jerusalem about threescore furlongs. And they talked together of all these things which had happened. And it came to pass, that, while they communed together and reasoned, Jesus himself drew near, and went with them. But their eyes were holden that they should not know him.
And it came to pass, as he sat at meat with them, he took bread, and blessed it, and brake, and gave to them. And their eyes were opened, and they knew him; and he vanished out of their sight. And they said one to another, Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?
They walked with the risen Lord and did not see Him. Sometimes grief is like that. But He was with them the whole way. Looking back, they could feel it. Their hearts had been burning.

application.text: First, think of one person you have lost, or one pain you carry. Take it to the Lord in prayer this week. Ask Him to help you see it through the hope of the Resurrection. Second, read Luke 24 slowly, all the way through. Notice how the disciples change from fear to joy. Third, share your hope with someone who is grieving. You do not need many words. You can say, “Death is not the end,” and stay with them.

closingVerse.text: And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.

opening.text: Walk past a tree in January. The branches are bare. The bark is gray. It looks dead, and no one would blame you for thinking so. Then spring comes. The buds swell. The leaves open. The tree was never dead. It was waiting.
A tree is only a picture. We do not rise each spring. We rise once, and we rise for good. But I think God put that picture in the world on purpose. It points to something much greater.
I want to talk about the Resurrection of Jesus Christ. It is the reason winter does not win.

mainMessage.text: On the third day after He was crucified, Jesus rose from the dead. He did not come back as a spirit or a memory. He came back with a living, glorified body. Because of Him, the grave will give up every person who has ever lived. That truth changes how we face loss. It changes how we face our own end. And it tells us that our bodies and our lives are not temporary things that fade. They are meant to last.

blocks.text: The grave could not keep Him.

The women who went to the tomb that morning were not looking for a miracle. They were going to finish a sad job. What they found changed the world. The stone was moved. The body was gone. And an angel asked them why they were looking for a living person among the dead.

Now upon the first day of the week, very early in the morning, they came unto the sepulchre, bringing the spices which they had prepared, and certain others with them. And they found the stone rolled away from the sepulchre. And they entered in, and found not the body of the Lord Jesus. And it came to pass, as they were much perplexed thereabout, behold, two men stood by them in shining garments: And as they were afraid, and bowed down their faces to the earth, they said unto them, Why seek ye the living among the dead? He is not here, but is risen: remember how he spake unto you when he was yet in Galilee,

The Savior was the only one who could accomplish this. From His mother He inherited power to die. From His Father He obtained power over death.
The grave was never going to hold Him. He laid down His life, and He took it up again.
The risen Lord had a body you could touch.
The first disciples struggled to believe it, too. When Jesus appeared to them, they were frightened. They thought He was a spirit. Jesus did not argue. He invited them to touch Him and see.

And as they thus spake, Jesus himself stood in the midst of them, and saith unto them, Peace be unto you. But they were terrified and affrighted, and supposed that they had seen a spirit. And he said unto them, Why are ye troubled? and why do thoughts arise in your hearts? Behold my hands and my feet, that it is I myself: handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have.
Thomas missed that first visit. He wanted proof of his own. Jesus gave it to him, kindly, and then spoke a blessing for the rest of us.

Then saith he to Thomas, Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing. And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God. Jesus saith unto him, Thomas, because thou hast seen me, thou hast believed: blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed.
Elder Joseph B. Wirthlin of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles spoke about what this gift means for us in his talk “Christians in Belief and Action” from the October 1996 general conference.

As part of the Atonement, the Savior overcame physical death and provided immortality for every one of God’s children through the Resurrection. He also overcame spiritual death and provided the possibility of eternal life, the life that God lives and the greatest of all the gifts of God.
That is a promise with no fine print. Every one of God’s children is included.
This gift is for everyone.

Some gifts are earned. This one is not. The prophets in the Book of Mormon said the Resurrection will reach the old and the young, the rich and the poor, the good and the not so good. What changes after that is the judgment. But the rising is for all.

Now, there is a death which is called a temporal death; and the death of Christ shall loose the bands of this temporal death, that all shall be raised from this temporal death. The spirit and the body shall be reunited again in its perfect form; both limb and joint shall be restored to its proper frame, even as we now are at this time; and we shall be brought to stand before God, knowing even as we know now, and have a bright recollection of all our guilt. Now, this restoration shall come to all, both old and young, both bond and free, both male and female, both the wicked and the righteous; and even there shall not so much as a hair of their heads be lost; but every thing shall be restored to its perfect frame, as it is now, or in the body, and shall be brought and be arraigned before the bar of Christ the Son, and God the Father, and the Holy Spirit, which is one Eternal God, to be judged according to their works, whether they be good or whether they be evil.

The soul shall be restored to the body, and the body to the soul; yea, and every limb and joint shall be restored to its body; yea, even a hair of the head shall not be lost; but all things shall be restored to their proper and perfect frame.
Elder Dallin H. Oaks of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this in his talk “All Men Everywhere” from the April 2006 general conference.

We . . . read that ‘his blood atoneth for the sins of those . . . who have died not knowing the will of God concerning them, or who have ignorantly sinned’ (Mosiah 3:11). Similarly, ‘the blood of Christ atoneth for \[little children\]’ (Mosiah 3:16). His grace is for all. That includes you, and it includes the people you worry about.
Grief is real, and so is hope.

Death still hurts. Jesus wept at a grave Himself. The gospel does not ask us to pretend the pain is small. It asks us to see the pain in a bigger light. Abinadi said the grave has no victory. Paul said death is swallowed up in victory.

And if Christ had not risen from the dead, or have broken the bands of death that the grave should have no victory, and that death should have no sting, there could have been no resurrection. But there is a resurrection, therefore the grave hath no victory, and the sting of death is swallowed up in Christ.

So when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory. O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory? The sting of death is sin; and the strength of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.
Elder Russell M. Nelson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles gave this counsel in his talk “Now Is the Time to Prepare” from the April 2005 general conference.

Brothers and sisters, we live to die and we die to live—in another realm. If we are well prepared, death brings no terror. From an eternal perspective, death is premature only for those who are not prepared to meet God. Now is the time to prepare. Then, when death comes, we can move toward the celestial glory that Heavenly Father has prepared for His faithful children. He did not say the sting disappears at once. He said it is soothed. That is an honest word, and a kind one.
What is broken will be mended.

We live in bodies that wear out. Knees ache. Eyes dim. Some people are born with limits they never chose. The Resurrection tells us that none of that is permanent. President Joseph F. Smith saw the spirit world, and he saw how the Lord’s work there looked ahead to the day of rising.

Their sleeping dust was to be restored unto its perfect frame, bone to his bone, and the sinews and the flesh upon them, the spirit and the body to be united never again to be divided, that they might receive a fulness of joy.
Elder Russell M. Nelson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles spoke about our progress in his talk “Perfection Pending” from the October 1995 general conference.

If you feel tired of trying, hear this. You are not behind. Perfection is pending, and it comes through Him.
He is the one who gives life.
Before He rose, Jesus told Martha who He was. She was grieving. He did not give her an argument. He gave her Himself.

Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live: And whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die. Believest thou this?
Paul called Him the firstfruits. The first harvest is a promise that more is coming.

But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept. For since by man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.
Elder D. Todd Christofferson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles spoke of the Resurrection as part of the plan in his talk “The Blessing of Scripture” from the April 2010 general conference.

The central purpose of all scripture is to fill our souls with faith in God the Father and in His Son, Jesus Christ—faith that They exist; faith in the Father’s plan for our immortality and eternal life; faith in the Atonement and Resurrection of Jesus Christ, which animates this plan of happiness; faith to make the gospel of Jesus Christ our way of life; and faith to come to know ‘the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom \[He has\] sent’ (John 17:3).
The word is “animates.” The Resurrection gives the plan its life.

story.title: Lazarus comes forth

blocks.text: Lazarus had been in the tomb four days. His sisters, Mary and Martha, had sent for Jesus, and He had come too late, or so it seemed. Jesus wept. Then He went to the tomb and called out.

And when he thus had spoken, he cried with a loud voice, Lazarus, come forth. And he that was dead came forth, bound hand and foot with graveclothes: and his face was bound about with a napkin. Jesus saith unto them, Loose him, and let him go.

This was not the Resurrection. Lazarus would die again. But it showed what the Savior can do. He spoke, and the dead heard Him. Notice, too, what He said next: “Loose him, and let him go.” He wants us free.

application.text: First, name one fear you have about death or loss. Write it down, then pray about it. Ask for the peace that comes from knowing He lives. Second, spend time with someone who is old, sick or grieving. Listen more than you talk. Third, this week, read 1 Corinthians 15 aloud. Let Paul’s joy become yours.

opening.text: Think of a glove. By itself it is just cloth. It lies on a table and does nothing. Put a hand inside, and it moves. It grips. It does work. Take the hand out, and the glove goes limp.

Think of the spirit as the hand and the body as the glove. It is not a perfect picture, because our body is far more than cloth. But it helps. A spirit without a body is limited. And for a time, death separates the two.
The Resurrection of Jesus Christ puts them back together. This time it is for good.

mainMessage.text: Jesus Christ was crucified and laid in a tomb. On the third day He came out alive, with a body of flesh and bone made perfect. He is the first to rise in this way. Because of His gift, every one of us will be reunited, spirit and body, never to be separated again. This is not a vague hope. It is a promise from the One who kept it first. And it makes the hard things we face now much easier to carry.

blocks.text: The tomb stood open.

The sting is taken out.

A bee sting hurts because of the poison it leaves. Death has had a sting too. It is the loneliness of the empty chair and the silence in the house. The scriptures say that sting does not get the last word.

And if Christ had not risen from the dead, or have broken the bands of death that the grave should have no victory, and that death should have no sting, there could have been no resurrection. But there is a resurrection, therefore the grave hath no victory, and the sting of death is swallowed up in Christ.

So when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory. O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory? The sting of death is sin; and the strength of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.
Elder Russell M. Nelson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles offered comfort in his talk “Now Is the Time to Prepare” from the April 2005 general conference.

Brothers and sisters, we live to die and we die to live—in another realm. If we are well prepared, death brings no terror. From an eternal perspective, death is premature only for those who are not prepared to meet God. Now is the time to prepare. Then, when death comes, we can move toward the celestial glory that Heavenly Father has prepared for His faithful children. Meanwhile, for sorrowing loved ones left behind . . . the sting of death is soothed by a steadfast faith in Christ, a perfect brightness of hope, a love of God and of all men, and a deep desire to serve them.
Notice what soothes the sting. Faith in Christ. Hope. Love. Service. Those are things we can do today.
The body will be perfect.

We may look at our bodies with frustration. Some of us have pain every day. Some of us grieve over what we or our children can’t do. The Resurrection does not ask us to hide our struggle. It tells us the struggle has an end. In a vision, President Joseph F. Smith saw the spirits of the righteous waiting for that day.

Their sleeping dust was to be restored unto its perfect frame, bone to his bone, and the sinews and the flesh upon them, the spirit and the body to be united never again to be divided, that they might receive a fulness of joy.
Elder Russell M. Nelson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles gave a gentle reminder in his talk “Perfection Pending” from the October 1995 general conference.

We need not be dismayed if our earnest efforts toward perfection now seem so arduous and endless. Perfection is pending. It can come in full only after the Resurrection and only through the Lord. It awaits all who love him and keep his commandments.
Spirit and body, joined “never again to be divided.” That is the fulness of joy the Lord has in mind for us.
He is the resurrection.
Notice how Jesus put it. He did not say, “I will give resurrection.” He said, “I am the resurrection.” It is not only a thing He does. It is who He is.

Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live: And whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die. Believest thou this?
And Paul explained how we fit into the story. He rose first. We follow.

But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept. For since by man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.
Elder D. Todd Christofferson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said this in his talk “The Blessing of Scripture” from the April 2010 general conference.

The central purpose of all scripture is to fill our souls with faith in God the Father and in His Son, Jesus Christ—faith that They exist; faith in the Father’s plan for our immortality and eternal life; faith in the Atonement and Resurrection of Jesus Christ, which animates this plan of happiness; faith to make the gospel of Jesus Christ our way of life; and faith to come to know ‘the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom \[He has\] sent’ (John 17:3).
Faith in the Resurrection is not a side belief. It is at the heart of the plan.

story.title: The widow’s son at Nain

blocks.text: A widow in the town of Nain was walking to bury her only son. She had already lost her husband. Now she had lost the one person who was supposed to care for her. She did not ask Jesus for anything. He saw her anyway.

Now when he came nigh to the gate of the city, behold, there was a dead man carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow: and much people of the city was with her. And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her, and said unto her, Weep not. And he came and touched the bier: and they that bare him stood still. And he said, Young man, I say unto thee, Arise. And he that was dead sat up, and began to speak. And he delivered him to his mother.
The last line is the one I love. He delivered him to his mother. The Resurrection is not only power. It is the Lord giving people back to the ones who love them.

opening.text: Have you ever watched the sky before sunrise? It is the darkest part of the night, or it feels that way. You cannot see the road. You cannot see the hills. Then a thin line of light shows on the edge of the world. It grows. And the whole landscape comes back, as if it had never left.
The disciples of Jesus lived through the darkest night of their lives. Their Teacher was dead. Their hopes were buried. And then, early on a Sunday, the light came.
That light is the Resurrection of Jesus Christ. I would like to talk about it today.

mainMessage.text: The Savior died on the cross and was buried. On the third day He rose, alive, in a glorified body that people could see and touch. He did this for every person who has ever lived. We are among those who have not seen, and yet have believed. The Lord called us blessed.

He is the light of the morning.
Jesus told Martha what the sunrise would be. It would be Him.

Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live: And whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die. Believest thou this?

story.title: Jairus’s daughter

blocks.text: Jairus was a leader in the synagogue. His little girl was twelve, and she was dying. He fell at the feet of Jesus and begged Him to come. On the way, people from his house told him it was too late. She was gone. Jesus told him not to be afraid. Then He went into the room.

And he took the damsel by the hand, and said unto her, Talitha cumi; which is, being interpreted, Damsel, I say unto thee, arise. And straightway the damsel arose, and walked; for she was of the age of twelve years. And they were astonished with a great astonishment.

Think about that moment. A father who thought his hope was gone. A hand. A word. A child who stood up and walked. That is a small picture of what He will do for every family on the morning of the Resurrection.

opening.text: A farmer puts a seed in the ground. It is small and dry. It does not look like much. He covers it with soil, and for a while nothing happens. Anyone passing by would think he had buried something dead.
Then a green shoot comes up. In time, there is a plant, taller and fuller than the seed ever was. Nothing was lost. The seed became more than it was.

I don’t want to push this picture too far. But Paul used a seed to teach about the Resurrection, and I think it fits. Today I want to talk about how Jesus Christ rose from the grave, and what that means for us.

mainMessage.text: Jesus was buried, and on the third day He rose. He did not rise as a spirit. He rose in a perfect body, and He was seen by many. His Resurrection is the first of its kind, and it opens the way for all of us. Everyone who has lived will rise. Our bodies will be restored to a perfect frame, joined again to our spirits. This should change how we feel about loss and about our own lives.

Now upon the first day of the week, very early in the morning, they came unto the sepulchre, bringing the spices which they had prepared, and certain others with them. One of the most tender parts of the story is how Jesus handled their doubts. He did not demand faith. He offered evidence. He showed His wounds. He ate with them. He let them touch Him.

Life does not come from the grave. It comes from Him. He told Martha so, in the middle of her grief.

Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live: And whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die. Believest thou this?

story.title: The Savior appears to the Nephites

blocks.text: After His Resurrection, Jesus visited the people in the Americas. They gathered at the temple in Bountiful, and a voice came from heaven. Then they saw a man descending, in a white robe. He stood in the midst of them and spoke. He invited them to come to Him one at a time.

And it came to pass that the Lord spake unto them saying: Arise and come forth unto me, that ye may thrust your hands into my side, and also that ye may feel the prints of the nails in my hands and in my feet, that ye may know that I am the God of Israel, and the God of the whole earth, and have been slain for the sins of the world. And it came to pass that the multitude went forth, and thrust their hands into his side, and did feel the prints of the nails in his hands and in his feet; and this they did do, going forth one by one until they had all gone forth, and did see with their eyes and did feel with their hands, and did know of a surety and did bear record, that it was he, of whom it was written by the prophets, that should come.

There were about twenty-five hundred people there. He did not rush. He let each one come. That is how personal the Resurrection is. It is not a doctrine for crowds. It is a Savior who knows each name.

closingVerse.text: Verily, verily, I say unto you, That ye shall weep and lament, but the world shall rejoice: and ye shall be sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy. And ye now therefore have sorrow: but I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and your joy no man taketh from you.
